---
title: "EBMF versus cNMF: scores, loadings and reproducibility"
description: "A bounded PBMC case study of prior support, factor matching, cell subsampling and residual variance."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

Compare scores and loadings separately before calling a program reproducible.
This case study uses **180 PBMC3k cells and 300 selected genes**.
It illustrates a comparison workflow; it does not establish a method winner.

```{r case-setup, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 144)
case_dir <- file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)), "data")
stability <- read.csv(file.path(case_dir, "ebmf-cnmf-stability.csv"))
stability$qualified <- as.logical(stability$qualified)
stopifnot(!anyNA(stability$qualified))
fit_summary <- read.csv(file.path(case_dir, "ebmf-cnmf-fits.csv"))
noise_summary <- read.csv(file.path(case_dir, "ebmf-cnmf-noise.csv"))
matching_summary <- read.csv(file.path(case_dir, "ebmf-cnmf-matching.csv"))
```

## Which factorization are we comparing?

Write the approximation as \(Y\approx LF^T\). Rows of \(L\) describe
cell activities. Rows of \(F\) describe gene effects.

| Model | Cell-score prior | Gene-effect prior | Allowed interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signed EBMF | normal | point-Laplace | Signed activities and opposing gene effects |
| Semi-nonnegative EBMF | point-exponential | point-Laplace | Positive activities with opposing gene effects |
| Nonnegative EBMF | point-exponential | point-exponential | Additive positive activities and gene effects |
| cNMF | Nonnegative optimization | Nonnegative spectra | Additive positive usages and spectra |

The nonnegative EBMF arm is the closest support control against cNMF.
Its shrinkage, likelihood and optimizer still differ from cNMF.
Point-Laplace has a prior spike at zero. That does not guarantee many
exact zeros in posterior means, or fewer selected genes than point-normal.

Raw scores in both methods need not sum to one. cNMF's `load_results`
normally returns normalized usages. Use raw usages with their corresponding
spectra when checking reconstruction. Avoid comparing normalized usages
with raw EBMF scores as though their amplitudes had the same meaning.

An explicit feature intercept gives \(Y_{ij}\approx\mu_j+\sum_kL_{ik}F_{jk}\).
Then signed effects describe changes in transformed coordinates, conditional
on the baseline and other factors. They are not negative abundances.
**The fitted results below have no explicit intercept.** Adding one is a
separate sensitivity; it changes component capacity and program allocation.

## Keep the data comparison explicit

The common-input experiment fits all methods to the same nonnegative matrix:
the same cells, 300 genes and variance-scaled normalized counts.
The EBMF baseline supplies `S=1` and estimates pooled additional variance.
All EBMF fits use greedy addition, backfitting and nullchecking.

We set EBMF `Kmax=12` and supply cNMF `K=12`. These are supplied limits,
not evidence that either method selected an optimal rank. Each EBMF run is
an individual fit. Each cNMF run is a five-start consensus, with five
independent runs per method. cNMF uses `max_NMF_iter=300` and
`density_threshold=2.0`, which excludes no spectral outliers.
This reduced cNMF configuration is a diagnostic pilot.

A production cNMF analysis should inspect its K and distance diagnostics.
Use a justified density threshold and more consensus starts, such as
50--100. The example threshold `0.01` is not universally suitable.
See the [upstream cNMF workflow](https://github.com/dylkot/cNMF).

```{r common-input-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(subset(fit_summary, track == "common"), digits = 4,
             caption = "Common-input fits: actual ranks and relative training SSE.")
```

Training SSE measures reconstruction of the fitting matrix. It does not
measure held-out prediction, biological coherence or uncertainty calibration.
Do not compare SSE across different transformed input matrices.

## Match factors without inventing agreement

Factor order and reciprocal scaling are arbitrary. Normalize each loading
vector to length one and multiply its scores by the removed length.
Find a one-to-one assignment using loading cosine similarity.
Retain weak matches, inactive factors and unmatched factors.

A simultaneous score/loading sign flip is legal for fully signed EBMF.
It is not legal for a nonnegative score vector. Apply any valid orientation
change to both scores and loadings before comparing them.

For each matched pair, assess loading cosine, score correlation and score
amplitude differences on shared cells. Also check the full reconstructed
matrix. Two models can reconstruct similarly using split or rotated factors.
Joint-span coverage detects some of those relationships. It does not show
that a nonnegative-score model can express every algebraic combination.

## Starts and cell subsampling answer different questions

Five starts yield ten unordered within-method comparisons. These measure
initialization sensitivity on unchanged data. Five paired 80% cell subsamples
measure sensitivity to changing the cells. Each subsample is compared with
the full-data seed14 fit, using scores from the shared cells.

Genes, normalization and scaling stay fixed across these subsamples.
The results therefore condition on full-data preprocessing. The cells have
no independent donor labels for this analysis. These are neither donor
replication nor leakage-free predictive evaluations.

```{r stability-table, echo=FALSE}
aggregate_table <- aggregate(cbind(loading_cosine, score_correlation,
                                    score_relative_l2) ~ track + kind + model,
                              stability, median)
names(aggregate_table)[4:6] <- c("Loading cosine", "Score correlation",
                                "Relative score difference")
knitr::kable(aggregate_table, digits = 3,
             caption = "Medians across matched factors; weak and unmatched factors need separate review.")
```

The signed-score model agrees almost exactly across common-input starts.
Its cell-subsampling agreement is lower. The nonnegative-score models also
contain weak factor counterparts despite strong median start agreement.
A high median cannot establish reliability for every program.
One cNMF subsample run reports an iteration-limit warning in its underlying
NMF fits. Its comparisons remain in the table and have black rings.
These unqualified rows must not be mistaken for converged-fit evidence.

```{r match-denominators, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(matching_summary,
             caption = "Assignment denominators, including unmatched factors in either model.")
```

```{r score-loading-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="Each point is one matched factor from one cell subsample. Model-specific shapes supplement color. Black rings mark an underlying cNMF iteration cap. Loading cosine and score correlation can be low even when median agreement is high.", fig.cap="Loading agreement versus score agreement under five paired cell subsamples. Black rings mark the capped cNMF run. Points are dependent; they are not independent confidence-interval replicates."}
subsample_scores <- subset(stability, kind == "subsample")
ggplot(subsample_scores, aes(loading_cosine, score_correlation,
                            colour = model, shape = model)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = subset(subsample_scores, !qualified),
             aes(loading_cosine, score_correlation), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 1, colour = "black", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~track) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("cNMF" = "#AA3377", "Nonnegative EBMF" = "#228833",
    "Semi-nonnegative EBMF" = "#EE6677", "Signed EBMF" = "#4477AA")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.05, 1.02), ylim = c(-1.05, 1.05)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("cNMF" = 18, "Nonnegative EBMF" = 15,
    "Semi-nonnegative EBMF" = 17, "Signed EBMF" = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Matched loading cosine", y = "Score correlation", colour = NULL,
       shape = NULL) + theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Change the noise model deliberately

The [flashier single-cell tutorial](https://willwerscheid.github.io/flashier/articles/flashier_single_cell.html)
uses size-factor-normalized shifted-log counts. It supplies a small noise
floor and estimates gene-wise residual variance. We follow that recipe,
with **backfitting enabled**. Libraries use all 7,832 genes in the frozen
count object; the analysis then keeps the same 300 selected genes.

```{r tutorial-recipe, eval=FALSE}
# counts: cells x genes, before selecting the analysis genes.
size_factors <- rowSums(counts) / mean(rowSums(counts))
Y <- log1p(counts / size_factors)[, selected_genes, drop = FALSE]
set.seed(3)
s1 <- sd(log1p(rpois(1e7, 1 / nrow(Y))))

initializer <- function(flash) flashier::flash_greedy_init_default(
  flash, sign_constraints = c(1, 0), seed = 14
)
fit <- flashier::flash_init(as.matrix(Y), S = s1, var_type = 2)
fit <- flashier::flash_greedy(fit, Kmax = 12,
  ebnm_fn = list(ebnm::ebnm_point_exponential, ebnm::ebnm_point_laplace),
  init_fn = initializer, maxiter = 500)
fit <- flashier::flash_backfit(fit, maxiter = 500)
fit <- flashier::flash_nullcheck(fit, remove = TRUE)
```

Change both priors and initializer constraints for the other arms.
Use `c(1,1)` for the fully nonnegative arm and `c(0,0)` for the signed arm.
Save each native fit and its diagnostics rather than selecting the nicest run.

| `var_type` | Estimated variance structure |
|---|---|
| `0` | One pooled value |
| `1` | One value per cell |
| `2` | One value per gene |
| `c(1,2)` | Separable cell-by-gene structure |
| `NULL` | No estimated component; supplied `S` supplies all noise |

For estimated-variance models, flashier adds the learned variance to `S^2`.
Thus `S=1, var_type=0` is not fixed unit variance.
For this shifted-log dataset, the simulated floor is
`s1=0.051502549432030469`. It is tied to this transform and sample size.
Do not transfer that number unchanged to another measurement scale.
See the [native variance contract](https://willwerscheid.github.io/flashier/reference/flash.html).

```{r variance-grid, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(noise_summary, digits = 3,
             caption = "Variance/S sensitivity: include failed and capped fits in the requested denominator.")
```

Both signed-score cell-wise/no-floor starts failed in the EBNM optimizer.
Some separable-variance runs with the supplied floor also failed. Keep these failures in
the denominator. They are numerical outcomes for these recipes, not proof
that an entire prior family or variance structure is invalid.

The shifted-log models use different observation coordinates from the
common-input experiment. Compare their native loadings within that track.
For a cross-scale comparison, derive gene-association profiles from each
model's scores against one common observed matrix. Label those profiles
as associations; they are not interchangeable native gene effects.

## Does either method discover a missing program?

The earlier comparison used EBMF K12 against cNMF K4. The HLA/CD74 loading
direction had 86--88% of its squared loading mass outside the cNMF span.
With cNMF K12, that gap dropped to 16--20%. Rank accounted for much of
the apparent difference. The remaining gap does not establish novelty.

Some HLA/CD74 factors in the common-input nonnegative-score models are
concentrated on roughly two effective cells. Their poor subsampling matches
persist even though the highest-scoring cell remains in all five subsets.
Concentration is a warning about support; it is not a complete causal
explanation for the instability. Inspect both loading geometry and score
distribution before assigning a biological label.

A candidate private program needs a stable signature, support across
independent biological samples and evidence beyond an unmatched axis.
Review the joint target span, residual genes and possible split programs.
Treat positive and negative signatures separately for signed gene effects.
The previous constrained-loading metric had a sign-handling defect;
its old cone-coverage numbers are excluded from this case study.

## What remains unassessed?

No donor-held-out prediction, donor replication or calibrated discovery
uncertainty is established here. EB posterior summaries condition on the
fitted model; they do not replace refitting or biological replication.
The next scientific step is training-only preprocessing and fixed-signature
scoring of held-out donors, plus simulations with known signed/unsigned truth.

An explicit-intercept sensitivity also remains separate. Use
`fit_ebmf(..., intercept="feature", backfit=TRUE)` to protect its offset
during nullchecking. Count the offset when comparing total component
budgets. Do not silently add an offset to the archived no-intercept results.

## Reproducibility and credits

Results were generated on 2026-10-25 with R 4.5.1, flashier 1.0.60,
ebnm 1.1-42 and the pinned cNMF source revision
`5dbc5baaa0b9079b55bce554d801caa235a50457` in a cNMF 1.7.1 environment.
Initializer seeds are 14--18. Cell-subset seeds are 101--105.
Full fits, counts, source hashes, warnings and receipts remain in the local
scientific archive. This page carries compact derived summaries and does
not rerun either method during documentation builds.

PBMC3k data: **10x Genomics**. EBMF: **Wei Wang and Matthew Stephens**,
[JMLR (2021)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-589.html).
flashier: **Jason Willwerscheid, Peter Carbonetto, Wei Wang and Matthew Stephens**.
EBNM: **Jason Willwerscheid, Matthew Stephens and Peter Carbonetto**.
cNMF: **Dylan Kotliar and contributors**, [eLife (2019)](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.43803).
The variance-floor workflow adapts the credited flashier single-cell tutorial.
This comparison code and prose are independently written; upstream notices
remain intact. See the [full credits](https://github.com/mdmanurung/flashier-utils/blob/main/CREDITS.md).
